title: Run white-gas and propane camp stoves and pressure lanterns
summary: How to fill, pump, preheat and light white-gas, multi-fuel and propane camp stoves and pressure lanterns, keep the pump, O-rings and generator working, and handle mantles. A cold or flooded burner flares up, so light it outdoors with nothing that burns nearby. Never put petrol in a white-gas-only appliance, and never use any of them indoors or for heat: they make carbon monoxide.

materials.item: White gas (Coleman fuel, camp fuel, naphtha), or the fuel the appliance label names
Pump-cup oil or light mineral oil
Spare mantles of the right size
Spare generator and O-ring kit for the model
Soapy water for propane leak checks
1 lb (16.4 oz) propane cylinders, for propane stoves
Fire extinguisher, sand or a fire blanket

steps.text: Read the label: white-gas only, Dual Fuel, multi-fuel or propane. The Coleman lantern manual says Coleman fuel only; Coleman Dual Fuel stoves take Coleman fuel or unleaded petrol (Coleman fuel lantern, Coleman dual fuel). If an appliance isn't marked Dual Fuel, treat it as white gas only unless its label says otherwise.
steps.warn: Never kerosene or leaded fuel in a Dual Fuel stove, and never kerosene or car petrol in a Coleman white-gas lantern (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern). If the label says white gas only, no petrol.

steps.text: Fill outdoors with the appliance cold, the valve shut and no flame anywhere near. On a Coleman stove, take the tank off the stove first (Coleman dual fuel). Fill only to the fill line so there is air space, close the cap tight and wipe up spills (Coleman fuel lantern, MSR WhisperLite).
steps.warn: Never fill, loosen the cap or take off the tank while it is lit, hot, or near any flame, including pilot lights (Coleman fuel lantern, Coleman dual fuel).

steps.text: Before every use, look for fuel on the tank, pump, fuel line and burner and on the ground under it. Don't light it if you see or smell fuel (MSR WhisperLite).
steps.warn: In freezing weather O-rings stiffen and leak fuel. Check again after pumping and after lighting (MSR WhisperLite).

steps.text: Set it on level ground outdoors, with nothing that burns within 1.2 m (4 ft) and spare fuel at least 7.6 m (25 ft) away (MSR WhisperLite). Keep the connected fuel bottle as far from the burner as its line allows, and don't put a windscreen round it, use a pot wider than 25 cm (10 in) or run two stoves together: any of these can make the bottle explode (MSR WhisperLite).

Pump it: open the pump knob one turn, cover its hole with your thumb and give about 30 full strokes, then close the knob (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern). A half-empty MSR bottle needs 30–40 strokes, a full one 20–30, until it pushes back firmly (MSR WhisperLite).

Preheat a multi-fuel stove: let out about half a spoonful of fuel into the priming cup, close the valve and light the cup. A brief flame the size of a soccer ball is normal. After about 2 minutes, as it dies down, open the valve half a turn for a blue flame (MSR WhisperLite).
steps.warn: Never prime with extra fuel, and keep your face and body out from over the stove (MSR WhisperLite).

steps.text: Light a Coleman stove: lighting lever up, a lit match at the burner, then open the fuel valve quickly at least two turns. After a full minute put the lever down and pump in more pressure (Coleman dual fuel).
Light a lantern: with the mantles already burned in, push a lit match through the lighting hole and turn the fuel valve to high (Coleman fuel lantern).

If a stove keeps a tall yellow flame, or a lantern shows flame anywhere but the mantles, close the fuel valve and let it burn out and cool. Tip a stove upside down to empty the burner, wipe it dry and start again (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern).
steps.warn: Wait at least 5 minutes before relighting a hot stove, and never move one that is burning or hot (MSR WhisperLite).

steps.text: Keep the pressure up as it burns: about 10 strokes every 10 minutes on an MSR-type bottle (MSR WhisperLite).

Turn it off at the fuel valve. The flame lingers a few minutes on a stove (Coleman dual fuel), and a lantern dims and goes out in 1–2 minutes (Coleman fuel lantern). Let it cool 5 minutes before disconnecting or moving it (MSR WhisperLite).
Oil the pump cup now and then with pump-cup oil or mineral oil, and replace cracked cups and O-rings (Coleman dual fuel, MSR WhisperLite, MSR maintenance).
Fit a new generator when a lantern won't turn down or a stove runs badly on one brand of petrol (Coleman fuel lantern, Coleman dual fuel).

Change mantles outdoors: tie the new one on, light its bottom evenly and let it burn out (Coleman fuel lantern). The first burn puts material into the air (ORAU mantles), so as a precaution stand back from the smoke, keep the old ash away from food and children, and wash your hands after.
steps.warn: Older and some imported mantles contain radioactive thorium (EPA consumer products); the danger is breathing in or swallowing the dust (JSP 392).

steps.text: On a propane stove, screw the cylinder hand-tight into the regulator and brush soapy water on every joint before lighting. Growing bubbles mean a leak: check it isn't cross-threaded, tighten it and test again. If it still leaks, take the cylinder off (Coleman propane stove).
steps.warn: Never test with a flame, and never refill a disposable cylinder (Coleman propane stove).

notes:
## How a pressure stove or lantern works

A white-gas stove or lantern is a fuel tank you pump up with air, so the pressure pushes fuel to the burner. On the way it runs through a tube, the generator, which on a Coleman stove passes into the mixing chamber above the burner (Coleman dual fuel). The generator has to be hot before the burner runs properly. An MSR stove that isn't preheated enough burns with erratic yellow flames (MSR WhisperLite), and a Coleman stove with a tall yellow flame that won't settle is flooded or leaking (Coleman dual fuel). That is what a flare-up is: liquid fuel reaching a burner that isn't ready for it.

Coleman stoves start with a lighting lever that you hold up for the first minute, and Coleman lanterns are lit with a match pushed through a lighting hole (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern). MSR-type multi-fuel stoves have a separate fuel bottle and pump, and you preheat by burning a little fuel in a priming cup under the burner (MSR WhisperLite). On a lantern, part of the brightness control sits inside the generator, so a lantern that won't turn down usually needs a new generator (Coleman fuel lantern).

## Which fuel goes in what

| Appliance | Takes | Never |
|---|---|---|
| Coleman white-gas lantern (not marked Dual Fuel) | Coleman fuel (white gas, naphtha) | Kerosene or automotive fuel (Coleman fuel lantern). For a white-gas stove, the label decides |
| Coleman Dual Fuel stove | Coleman fuel or unleaded petrol | Kerosene or leaded fuel (Coleman dual fuel) |
| MSR WhisperLite Universal-type multi-fuel stove | White gas or unleaded petrol (one jet), kerosene (another jet), butane/propane canisters (a third jet) | Leaded fuel (MSR WhisperLite) |
| Propane camp stove | 1 lb (16.4 oz) disposable propane cylinders | A refilled disposable cylinder (Coleman propane stove) |

In Canada white gas is also called naphtha (MSR WhisperLite). Read the burner's label and the fuel can before you pour. The label on the appliance decides, not the shape of the tank.

Petrol from a car is a last resort even where it is allowed. It varies in quality and wears out generators (Coleman dual fuel), and on MSR stoves anything but white gas clogs the jet and fuel line faster and unleaded can shorten the stove's life (MSR WhisperLite, MSR maintenance). If you must, use the lowest grade of unleaded: premium blends carry more additives that clog (MSR maintenance).

## Lighting and flare-ups

- Light it outdoors, on level ground, with nothing that burns within 1.2 m (4 ft) of the top and sides and no fuel cans or open fuel within 7.6 m (25 ft) (MSR WhisperLite). Coleman gives 1.2 m (4 ft) above and 30 cm (1 ft) to the sides for its stoves and lanterns (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern).
- Keep your face and body out from over the stove while priming and lighting (MSR WhisperLite).
- When priming an MSR-type stove, a brief flame the size of a soccer ball is normal (MSR WhisperLite). A flame that keeps roaring high and yellow on a Coleman stove means it is flooded or leaking (Coleman dual fuel); on a lantern, any flame away from the mantles means the same (Coleman fuel lantern).
- What to do: close the fuel valve, let the flames burn out and the appliance cool. On a stove, turn it upside down to tip out fuel in the burner and wipe it dry, then start again (Coleman dual fuel).
- Don't relight a hot stove: wait at least 5 minutes, or it can light with a large flame (MSR WhisperLite). Never move a burning or hot stove (MSR WhisperLite).
- Too much priming fuel can leak or spill and start a fire, so use only the half-spoonful the maker says (MSR WhisperLite).

## Pump, O-rings and generator care

- **Pump cup:** the seal on the end of the pump plunger. A dry or damaged cup won't build pressure (MSR maintenance). Oil it now and then (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern), with pump-cup oil or any mineral oil (MSR WhisperLite). A cracked cup gets replaced (MSR maintenance).
- **Check valve:** the one-way valve inside the pump base. You should hear it open as you pump. If it leaks, fuel gets into the pump and dries the cup out (MSR maintenance).
- **O-rings:** look for nicks, cracks or dryness and lube them with pump-cup oil (MSR maintenance, MSR WhisperLite). In freezing weather O-rings stiffen and leak fuel, so check for leaks before and after pumping, priming and lighting (MSR WhisperLite). MSR says to service the jet and fuel line at least once a year (MSR WhisperLite).
- **Generator:** the commonest wear part. On a lantern, turning the valve from high to off to high a few times cleans the tip (Coleman fuel lantern). If a stove misbehaves on one brand of petrol, fit a new generator and change fuel (Coleman dual fuel). On MSR stoves, don't bend the generator loop when you take the jet out (MSR WhisperLite).
- **Tank:** rinse it with fresh fuel to flush out sediment, gum and water: twice a year for a stove, and once a year for a lantern kept for emergencies (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern).

## Mantles

A mantle is a small fabric sock that you tie onto the burner and burn once before use (Coleman fuel lantern). What is left glows in the flame (ORAU mantles). After that first burn it is very fragile: touching it with a finger or a match, or dropping the lantern, will break it (Coleman fuel lantern). Carry spares. Replace any mantle with a hole in it: a hole lets the flame overheat the lantern (Coleman fuel lantern).

**Thorium.** From the 1880s mantles were made with thorium, which is radioactive (ORAU mantles). Coleman switched to non-radioactive yttrium around 1990, but around 2000 about half the mantles sold in the US still contained thorium (ORAU mantles). Old stock in a garage, and some imported mantles, may still contain it (EPA consumer products). The radiation from a whole mantle is small: EPA does not consider it a significant health risk unless mantles are your main light source (EPA consumer products), which in a long outage they might be. The harm comes from inside the body: thorium dust breathed in or swallowed (JSP 392). The first burn of a new thorium mantle also releases radioactive decay products into the air, and ORAU says about half of the beryllium some mantles contain becomes airborne on that first heating (ORAU mantles). So:

- Burn in new mantles outdoors and stand back from the smoke.
- Don't crush, blow on or play with broken mantles and their ash; keep them away from food and children.
- Wash your hands after changing a mantle. UK defence rules require the same after work with thorium dust (JSP 392).
- Treat unmarked old mantles as if they contain thorium.

## Propane camp stoves

A propane camp stove screws a 1 lb (16.4 oz) disposable cylinder into a regulator set at the factory; don't try to adjust it (Coleman propane stove). Fit the cylinder hand-tight, check every joint with soapy water before lighting (growing bubbles mean a leak; never use a flame), and expect a blue flame with a hint of yellow at the tips (Coleman propane stove). Take the cylinder off whenever the stove is put away, and store cylinders away from heat and sun, below 49 °C (120 °F) (Coleman propane stove). The smell added to propane can fade, so don't rely on your nose alone (Coleman propane stove). Never refill a disposable cylinder (Coleman propane stove).

Propane boils at about −42 °C (−44 °F) (NIST propane), so it keeps working in cold that stops butane.

## Indoors and heat

Coleman's white-gas stoves and lanterns, Coleman's propane stove and MSR's multi-fuel stove are all for outdoor use only. Their makers say never use them inside a house, camper or tent, because they burn up oxygen and make carbon monoxide (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern, Coleman propane stove, MSR WhisperLite). Coleman also says never use the stove or lantern as a space heater (Coleman dual fuel, Coleman fuel lantern). CDC lists lanterns and camping stoves among the things never to use inside a home, tent or camper (CDC power outage). Cook outside and carry the food in. See [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors) and [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## When it won't work

| Problem | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Won't pressurise | Dry or cracked pump cup, or a leaking check valve (MSR maintenance) |
| Pressurises, weak flame | Clogged jet, fuel line or filter (MSR maintenance) |
| Erratic yellow flame | Not preheated enough, clogged jet, or wrong jet for the fuel (MSR WhisperLite) |
| Lantern won't turn down | Worn generator (Coleman fuel lantern) |
| Fuel visible under pressure | Failed seal or O-ring: replace before use (MSR maintenance) |
